issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a male civilian-in-war-zone trauma profile, sexual objectification as a central trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it lacks support from memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other items consistently describe war-related threat, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory trauma memory rather than sexualized threat, making this trigger hard to integrate into the same trauma presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding as a trigger is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items. No memory, threat, or appraisal items reference water, drowning, environmental disaster, or any related theme. Given the otherwise interpersonal/war-threat profile, this trigger appears disconnected from the formulation.

issues.item: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the indexed trauma type. For a civilian in a war zone, water/flooding and alcohol smell are hard to reconcile with the threat, memory, and appraisal items unless there is some specific unreported trauma context linking them. The rest of the profile centers on generalized danger, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory recall, but these two triggers imply a different situational pattern that is not otherwise represented.

The maladaptive strategy set is partly disconnected from the rest of the formulation. Drug use is plausible as a broad coping strategy, but excessive exercise and concealing clothing suggest body-focused avoidance or managing visibility/safety in a specific way that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items presented. Given the strong Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies and Threat → Maladaptive Strategies links, these strategies should plausibly follow from the reported triggers and threat beliefs, but these two items do not clearly do so.

vignette:
Arjun was twenty-two when he was posted to a consulate in a city that, until then, he had only seen on maps. The war had been there for years, but his assignment felt like a career step, not a danger. One afternoon, while his driver took him back from a meeting, a mortar round struck the vehicle ahead of them. The blast wave shoved their car sideways. For a long moment there was only ringing, the smell of burnt metal and something sour and chemical, and the sight of a man stumbling out of the wrecked sedan with blood sheeting down his face. Arjun remembers every second of it in perfect, relentless detail. He can still smell the scorched upholstery, the cordite, the sweetish undertone of alcohol that had been spilled from a flask in the glove compartment. He cannot, however, find the words to tell anyone what it felt like. When his partner asks, he says “it was loud” and leaves it there. The event lasted maybe thirty seconds, but it carved a groove in his mind so deep that he relives it without warning—sometimes triggered by a truck backfiring, sometimes by nothing he can identify.

In the months that followed, Arjun finished his tour and returned to a desk posting in Washington, D.C. He is still a diplomat, still expected to attend receptions, to shake hands with strangers, to stand in crowded rooms where waiters circulate with trays of wine. What frightened him most, he later told his therapist, was how normal he looked while his insides were screaming. He has come to believe that he cannot trust safety—people tell him the war is over, that he is home, that no one is trying to kill him, and he knows they mean well, but their words feel hollow. The world, he is certain, is not safe. Strangers approaching him on the street or in the office hallway make his chest tighten; he watches their hands, reads their movements for threat. Every unexpected bang—a door slamming, a stack of files dropped—punches him back into that car. He has lost his faith. Not in God, exactly, but in the idea that people are good or that life makes sense. He looks at himself and thinks there must be something fundamentally wrong with him, something that made the mortar choose that street, that car, that moment. He has no future; he cannot picture himself at thirty, let alone married or with children.

To manage, Arjun has built a fortress of rituals. He exercises compulsively—running until his knees ache, lifting weights until his arms shake—because exhaustion is the only reliable silence. He smokes marijuana most evenings, not to feel good but to blur the edges of the flashbacks that come when he is alone and trying to fall asleep. At work, he wears dark, shapeless jackets and keeps his head down, certain that being noticed is dangerous. His partner has begun to ask why he never wants to go out, why he flinches when she touches him from behind, why he spends whole weekends running the same loop in the park. He cannot explain. The words do not exist.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a reception at the embassy. A guest’s cologne reminded him of the alcohol smell—just a fleeting similarity—and he excused himself to the bathroom, where he stood gripping the sink for ten minutes, throat tight, seeing the blood again. His supervisor noticed him swaying and quietly suggested he get help. He is terrified that admitting he needs help will confirm his intrinsic fault. But he is also, somewhere underneath the hopelessness, hoping that if someone else can look at what happened and not blame him, maybe he can learn to look at it too.
